title: From restructuring print to first-billion ARR
body:
## The opening prints: out of the restructuring window

When Nebius Group disclosed its earliest post-restructuring quarterly results through 2025, the numbers were, by design, modest. The company that emerged from Yandex N.V.'s 2024 corporate separation was not a going concern with a seasoned customer base and a stable revenue line — it was a Netherlands-domiciled holding company with a GPU-cluster footprint in European data centres, roughly $3.7 billion of cash from the restructuring settlement, and a thesis about what AI infrastructure demand would look like at scale.

The early 2025 quarters told a familiar build-ahead story. Revenue scaled from a small base as the company signed its initial cohort of enterprise AI customers, provisioned capacity in European data centres, and began the laborious work of converting contracted commitments into recognised revenue under IFRS. Management communicated the ramp in terms that investors in hyperscaler capex cycles would recognise: the upfront investment thesis, the long-lead-time nature of GPU procurement, and the customer prepayment dynamic that would eventually become the most structurally distinctive feature of Nebius's reported financials.

What distinguished Nebius from the broader AI-cloud cohort in this period was not the pace of early revenue — it was the scale of the infrastructure commitment being built ahead of it.

## August 2025: the capital event that reset the investment narrative

The most consequential single capital-markets event of Nebius's post-restructuring life arrived in August 2025, when the company closed a $700 million oversubscribed strategic equity placement from Accel, Nvidia, and certain accounts managed by Orbis Investments. [Source: Nebius Group IR, group.nebius.com]

The placement's oversubscription was itself a signal, but it was the Nvidia participation that carried the most structural weight. Nvidia was simultaneously Nebius's dominant GPU supplier and, from August 2025 forward, a strategic equity investor. That alignment created a form of circular reinforcement that investors in the AI-infrastructure cycle had learned to parse carefully: an equity stake gives Nvidia a financial interest in Nebius's capacity ramp succeeding, which in turn shapes GPU allocation priority — a scarce resource that had become as strategically important as any clause in an enterprise cloud contract.

Accel's participation arrived with governance consequences. The firm's Matt Weigand received observer rights concurrent with the investment, and at the August 2025 annual general meeting, Weigand and Arne Grimme — a De Brauw Blackstone Westbroek corporate M&A partner — were elected to the board as independent non-executive directors. The additions completed a governance architecture that combined Yandex-legacy institutional memory with oversight capabilities appropriate to a NASDAQ-listed AI infrastructure company executing what would become a $16–20 billion multi-year capex programme.

The $700 million placement funded the Q3–Q4 2025 infrastructure ramp that produced the numbers on which Nebius's investment case would ultimately rest.

## Q3 2025: the trajectory clarifies

By the third quarter of 2025, the shape of the ramp had become legible to investors tracking the company's disclosures. Annualised recurring revenue had approached approximately $700 million — a figure that, while still sub-scale relative to the guidance management would eventually set for FY2026, represented a meaningful acceleration from the early-year base. [Source: Nebius 6-K, SEC EDGAR]

The core AI cloud segment was growing faster than the consolidated entity, as Nebius's portfolio subsidiaries — Toloka AI's human-data labelling business, TripleTen's online tech-education platform, and Avride's autonomous-driving unit — contributed revenue at materially lower growth rates. The margin trajectory was also improving: the adjusted EBITDA margin for the core segment reached 19% in Q3, a data point that management would later reference in the context of the FY2026 margin target.

The Q3 print established a pattern that would define the equity's trading behaviour through the back half of 2025: each quarterly disclosure was read not for its absolute revenue number — still modest relative to peer-set benchmarks — but for the acceleration implied in the ARR trajectory and the physical capacity being brought online behind it.

## February 12, 2026: the earnings release as inflection event

The Q4 2025 and full-year results, released on February 12, 2026, reframed the entire preceding year as prologue.

Consolidated quarterly revenue came in at $227.7 million, representing 547% year-on-year growth. [Source: Nebius Group, Business Wire, February 12 2026](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260212534404/en/Nebius-Reports-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Year-2025-Financial-Results) The core AI cloud segment, isolated from portfolio subsidiaries, posted 802% year-on-year growth in the quarter. The exit ARR reached $1.25 billion, up from the approximate $700 million annualised run-rate of Q3.

The headline revenue figure was, on its own terms, a miss. Analyst consensus had stood at roughly $247 million; the reported $227.7 million fell short by approximately 8%. In practice, however, the market's reaction to that gap was subordinated to what management disclosed alongside it.

The Q4 adjusted EBITDA margin for the core segment reached 24%, up five percentage points from Q3's 19% exit. Operating cash flow in the quarter was $834 million against $227.7 million of revenue. The divergence — nearly four dollars of operating cash inflow for every dollar of recognised revenue — was the clearest expression of the customer prepayment dynamic Nebius had described throughout 2025. Enterprise AI customers booking large compute contracts prepay for capacity; the cash arrives before the associated revenue is recognised under IFRS conventions. The $834 million Q4 operating cash flow was not a trading profit — it was the advance-payment signature of a business whose customers were committing to capacity months before they would consume it.

Year-end cash stood at $3.7 billion. [Source: Nebius 20-F, SEC EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001513845/000110465925015480/tm257185d1_ex99-1.htm) Capex in Q4 alone approximated $2 billion — a 9x capex-to-revenue ratio reflecting the build-ahead-of-demand posture of a company acquiring AI processor inventory and data centre power well before the contracted revenue associated with that capacity had begun to flow through the income statement.

Active connected power at year-end was 170 megawatts, against more than 2 gigawatts of contracted power — a 12:1 ratio of contracted-to-active capacity that expressed both the scale of the FY2026 execution challenge and the forward-demand visibility that management was translating into guidance.

## The FY2026 guidance: the most aggressive public commitment in the peer set

The targets management set for FY2026 on February 12 placed Nebius in a category of its own among publicly listed AI-cloud peers.

| Metric | FY2025 (Q4 / Exit) | FY2026 Guidance |
|---|---|---|
| Quarterly revenue | $227.7M (+547% YoY) | — |
| Full-year revenue | — | $3.0–3.4B |
| Adj. EBITDA margin (core) | 24% (Q4 exit) | ~40% |
| Year-end ARR | $1.25B | $7–9B |
| Capex | ~$2B in Q4 alone | $16–20B |
| Connected power (active) | 170MW | 800MW–1GW |

Revenue guidance of $3.0 to $3.4 billion implied roughly seven-fold growth over full-year 2025. The adjusted EBITDA margin target of approximately 40% — against the 24% Q4 exit rate — implied a substantial operating-leverage inflection as fixed infrastructure costs were spread across a materially higher revenue base, with depreciation curves bending as previously capitalised assets entered productive service.

The ARR target of $7 to $9 billion, with more than half of that amount already contracted at the time of the guidance disclosure, provided a degree of demand-side visibility unusual in AI-cloud forward guidance. Contracted ARR is not recognised revenue — it is signed customer commitments, subject to delivery — but the greater-than-50% contracted share translated the FY2026 ARR range from a speculative pipeline estimate into something closer to an execution question: could Nebius deploy the capacity fast enough to satisfy commitments already on paper?

The physical dimension of the guidance was its most ambitious component. Scaling connected power from 170 megawatts at year-end 2025 to 800 megawatts to 1 gigawatt at year-end 2026 required concurrent execution across power utility agreements, real-estate procurement, hardware supply — contingent on Nvidia GPU allocation — and customer onboarding at a pace without clear precedent among public AI-cloud issuers. The capex envelope of $16 to $20 billion, against starting cash of $3.7 billion, presupposed significant additional financing, with the customer-prepayment cash dynamics serving as one structural bridge and the Nvidia strategic relationship providing the supply-chain alignment that made the physical ramp plausible.

## Seven quarters in: a compression without precedent in the peer set

Taken across the seven public quarters since the Nebius brand and strategy were established, the cumulative narrative is one of unusual compression. The company executed a corporate restructuring — separating a Russia-domiciled operating business from a Netherlands holding company and relisting on NASDAQ under a new ticker — while simultaneously rebuilding a balance sheet from settlement cash, constructing an AI-cloud infrastructure footprint, recruiting a customer base capable of generating $1.25 billion in ARR, and closing the most strategically consequential equity financing of its short public history.

The 547% Q4 revenue growth figure, striking in isolation, understated the transformation when viewed against the restructuring baseline. Nebius did not accelerate an existing AI-cloud business — it built one inside a restructured holding company while that company was simultaneously resolving its post-Yandex governance architecture and assembling the capital stack required to fund a $16–20 billion infrastructure programme.

The February 12, 2026 earnings release was the moment the sum of those parts became legible as a single coherent story: a corporate reorganisation that had, inside seven public quarters, become one of the most aggressive AI-infrastructure-capacity expansion narratives in the public-equity cycle.
